Meanwhile modern applications lean heavily on database caching to keep read latency low. A cache stores hot rows in memory, sparing the primary database repeated work; cached queries that once took many milliseconds now return quickly, and hardware budgets shrink.

However this speed carries real complexity. Every cache must answer a hard question: what happens when the underlying data changes? Stale entries can mislead users, corrupt downstream reports, and erode trust in the platform; teams therefore pair each cached value with an expiration policy, plus explicit invalidation hooks that fire whenever writers touch related tables.

Along with its gains, caching brings risk; an app can show old data if invalidation is sloppy. Solid tuning aids trust: apply short TTLs, drop old rows quickly, and monitor hit ratios against traffic that shifts throughout a day.

Finally treat your cache as a formal contract: measure hit rates, rehearse failure modes, and call the careful design done.
